diagnosis: Subacute combined degeneration due to vitamin B12 deficiency
mechanism: Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause demyelinating injury in the spinal cord, classically involving posterior (dorsal) columns and lateral corticospinal tracts. Posterior-column dysfunction causes impaired vibration/proprioception and sensory ataxia, whereas corticospinal involvement produces spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses.
vignette: A 61-year-old woman with autoimmune gastritis has progressive numbness of both feet and gait instability. Examination shows impaired vibration and joint-position sense in the legs, a positive Romberg sign, increased patellar reflexes, bilateral ankle clonus, and extensor plantar responses. Serum vitamin B12 is low and methylmalonic acid is elevated.
lead: Which pair of spinal cord pathways is most likely affected in this patient?
correct: Posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
distractors: Anterior spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn motor neurons
Lateral spinothalamic tracts and dorsal root entry zones
Anterior corticospinal tracts and intermediolateral cell columns
Spinocerebellar tracts and substantia gelatinosa only
distractor_notes: Anterior horn disease produces lower-motor-neuron weakness, and anterior spinothalamic injury affects crude touch; this does not explain simultaneous proprioceptive loss and upper-motor-neuron signs.
Lateral spinothalamic pathways carry pain and temperature. The dominant sensory deficit here is vibration/proprioception, and the patient also has corticospinal signs.
The lateral, not anterior, corticospinal tract is the major descending tract involved in classic subacute combined degeneration; intermediolateral columns are autonomic preganglionic regions.
Spinocerebellar pathways may be affected in some B12-deficiency cases, but they do not by themselves explain the posterior-column sensory loss plus corticospinal upper-motor-neuron findings.
key_expl: The combination of low vitamin B12, elevated methylmalonic acid, loss of vibration and joint-position sense, sensory ataxia, and upper-motor-neuron signs indicates subacute combined degeneration. The name 'combined' refers to simultaneous involvement of posterior columns and lateral columns, especially the lateral corticospinal tracts. Posterior-column demyelination impairs vibration and proprioception, while corticospinal demyelination causes spasticity, hyperreflexia, clonus, and Babinski signs.
objective: Localize vitamin B12–related subacute combined degeneration to the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts based on the combination of proprioceptive sensory loss and upper-motor-neuron signs.
clues: autoimmune gastritis with low vitamin B12
loss of vibration and joint-position sense
